CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male who presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Henry Howard, on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. Workup for headaches with brain MRI and serology incidentally revealed a pituitary lesion. The patient describes headaches located behind the eyes, characterized as a dull nagging ache. Onset was gradual approximately three months ago, starting at 3/10 severity and gradually worsening to 6/10 severity. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning and last a few hours at a time. Patient denies any measures that make headaches better or worse. He also reports recently bumping into door frames. MRI from 3/4/21 reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies nausea, fever, rashes, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. No reported change in vision per patient, though eye exam in fall was unremarkable. No reported balance changes.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. Patient denies any medical problems.

MEDICATIONS
Patient denies taking any medications. Tried acetaminophen a few times for headaches without relief and stopped.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and reports no known family history of diseases.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a house. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect appropriate and speech fluent. Cranial nerve examination grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 including CBC, CMP, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH; all other results normal. Brain MRI with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign-appearing pituitary adenoma with symptomatic optic chiasmal compression. Patient is a very pleasant 52-year-old male with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression; therefore surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated. Plan for transsphenoidal approach to surgery. Risks of anesthesia discussed including heart attack, stroke, and death. Risks of surgery discussed including infection, need for further surgery, wound issues such as spinal fluid leak, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, or death. Patient counseled that vision improvement is possible but not guaranteed. Referral placed for preoperative visual field testing by ophthalmology for comparison after surgery. Surgery scheduler to arrange surgical date and preoperative testing.
